Welcome to Biology 101. I'm Professor Martin, and this is my laboratory assistant, Peter Smith. This course meets twice a week for lecture and once a week for laboratory assignments. The text for this course is Introduction to Biological Sciences, by Abramson. You should get the text and read the first chapter before the next class. You will also need the laboratory manual. I've passed out a copy of the course syllabus. It lists the reading assignments and exam dates. We will cover one chapter a week for each of the next fifteen weeks, and there will be three exams. Grades in this course are based on your exam grades and on your grades for the laboratory assignments.

M

In yesterday's class, we discussed volcanoes located in the area known as the Ring of Fire, an area which basically encircles the Pacific. Most of the world's active volcanoes are located along the Ring of Fire, and the eruptions that take place there are among the most violent in the world. Today we're going to discuss the volcanoes of Hawaii, which are quite different from the volcanoes in the Ring of Fire. Hawaiian volcanoes are not located along the Ring of Fire. Instead, Hawaii is located in the middle of a massive plate. Hawaiian volcanoes are much gentler than those in the Ring of Fire. They have much less gas in them, which causes less explosive eruptions, and their lava is thinner, which results in mounds that are long and low rather than high and steep. Mauna Loa, the name of one of Hawaii's most famous volcanoes, actually means long mountain.

W

I hope you've enjoyed your visit so far in Washington, D.C. Today we're going on a tour of the Smithsonian. The Smithsonian is actually several museums, each with a different focus, situated together on a mall. These museums have more than sixty million items on exhibit. The first museum we'll visit is the Museum of Natural History, which has various types of stuffed animals and exhibits showing the life-styles of early American Indians and Eskimos. From there we'll go on to the National Air and Space Museum, where you can see the airplane that Orville Wright used to make his first flight. After we visit those two museums as a group, you'll have free time to visit some of the other Smithsonian museums: the Museum of American History, the Arts and Industries Building, and the various art museums. After our trip to the Smithsonian today, we'll go on to the White House tomorrow.
